headings.title: Introduction to the Internet and World Wide Web in Nursing
headings.content: The internet is a massive global network of interconnected computers, while the World Wide Web is a collection of webpages and documents accessible via that network using browsers. In modern Nigerian healthcare, these tools transform how nurses communicate, document, and access clinical guidelines. Patient care no longer relies solely on physical paper textbooks or local hospital notices; clinical updates travel instantly across digital platforms. Nurses use web portals for shift handovers, accessing national health policies from the Federal Ministry of Health, and coordinating patient referrals between tertiary centers and primary health clinics.

headings.title: Core Architecture: How the Internet Works in Healthcare Settings
headings.content:
Hospital internet connectivity relies on structured infrastructure including local area networks (LANs), Wi-Fi routers, and secure servers. Devices communicate using standardized protocols like TCP/IP, ensuring patient data packets travel accurately from the ward terminal to the electronic medical record (EMR) database without corruption. 

- **Routers**: Direct traffic between internal hospital departments and external networks.
- **Servers**: Centralized computers that store patient databases and clinical software.
- **Firewalls**: Security barriers that block unauthorized external access while permitting legitimate hospital traffic.

headings.title: Accessing and Searching Medical Literature
headings.content: Evidence-based practice requires nurses to locate credible research efficiently. Using databases such as PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar provides access to peer-reviewed journals and clinical trials. Effective literature searching utilizes boolean operators like AND, OR, and NOT to narrow or broaden search results. For instance, searching "malaria AND pregnancy" retrieves studies specifically addressing management in expectant mothers, filtering out irrelevant general articles on vector control.

headings.title: Telehealth, Telemedicine, and Remote Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Telehealth broadens healthcare delivery by utilizing telecommunications to bridge geographical gaps between patients and clinical teams. Telemedicine specifically refers to remote clinical services, allowing doctors and nurses to consult patients via video calls, phone text messages, or mobile apps. In rural Nigerian communities, remote patient monitoring devices track chronic conditions like hypertension and diabetes, transmitting vital signs directly to urban health facilities for timely nursing intervention.

headings.title: Internet Security, Privacy, and Patient Data Protection
headings.content: Protecting patient health information (PHI) is a fundamental duty for every nurse operating in digital environments. Cyber threats such as phishing, malware, and unauthorized database access threaten patient confidentiality. Nurses must use strong, unique passwords, log out of terminal stations when leaving the bedside, and avoid sharing patient photographs or clinical details on public social media platforms. Data encryption and compliance with local data protection regulations ensure sensitive medical histories remain private and secure.

headings.title: Evaluating Online Health Information for Clinical Accuracy
headings.content: The internet contains vast amounts of health-related content, much of which lacks scientific backing or peer review. Nurses must guide patients and critically appraise web sources using established criteria such as the CRAAP test (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, and Purpose). Reliable medical websites typically feature transparent authorship, clear references to scientific research, editorial review boards, and professional organizational backing rather than commercial product advertisements.

headings.title: Ethical and Legal Implications of Internet Use in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Digital tools introduce complex ethical dilemmas regarding professional boundaries, patient autonomy, and liability. Nurses face legal repercussions if they provide informal medical diagnoses via social media chat apps or violate patient confidentiality online. Professional codes of conduct apply equally to digital spaces; interacting inappropriately with patients on social networks or discussing specific clinical cases online breaches the trust inherent in the nurse-patient relationship.
